# Two unit positives and one fractional positive: an exact endpoint theorem

This is the repaired source. The first candidate had an incorrect positive-z substitution and is superseded entirely by this version. The verifier now starts from the actual density and checks that substitution explicitly.

For every integer m>=2 and p in[0,1], let

    P_m(p)=Pr(Gamma(2)+p Exp(1)
              >=Exp(1)+[(1+p)/m] Gamma(m)),

with all random variables independent. Then

    P_m(p)>=min{P_m(0),P_m(1)}.                       (1)

Both endpoints belong to the proved saturated-positive family. In particular its uniform bound gives P_m(p)>9/20. This note proves (1) for arbitrary m; it does not assert the analogous endpoint theorem with three or more positive units.

## 1. A density representation and the exact derivative

Let X be the fractional-positive unit exponential, let Y be the Gamma(m) variable, and put T=X+Y, U=X/T. Their joint gamma change of variables gives independence of T~Gamma(m+1) and U~Beta(1,m). Let W=Gamma(2)-Exp(1), independent of T,U, and put Z=W/T. Write b=(1+p)/m. The event is Z+(p+b)U-b>=0. Since Pr(U>=u)=(1-u)^m on[0,1], conditioning gives

    P_m(p)=Pr(Z>=b)
       +integral_(-p)^b [(p+z)/(p+b)]^m f_Z(z) dz.    (2)

The density of W is e^w/4 for w<0 and e^(-w)(1+2w)/4 for w>=0. Averaging T f_W(zT) gives

    f_Z(z)=(m+1)/[4(1-z)^(m+2)]                    (z<0),
    f_Z(z)=(m+1)[1+(2m+5)z]/[4(1+z)^(m+3)]        (z>=0).

Differentiating (2), the upper-endpoint terms cancel and the lower-endpoint term vanishes. On compact subintervals of p in(0,1) this is justified by the continuous density and the bounded continuous parameter derivative on the finite moving ranges. We obtain

    P_m'(p)=I_m(p)/(p+b)^(m+1),
    I_m(p)=integral_(-p)^b (p+z)^(m-1)
                        [1-(m+1)z] f_Z(z) dz.       (3)

Put r=m+1>=3 and define

    A(p)=(2r+3)p^2+(3r+1)p-r,
    D(p)=p^2+(3r+1)p+r+2,
    L(p)=4p^(r+1)(r+p)^(r+1)D(p)
          -(1+p)^2(1+rp)^(r+1)A(p).

Direct integration in (3) gives

    I_m(p)=L(p)/[4m(1-p)^3(1+p)^2(r+p)^(r+1)].       (4)

Here is the full algebraic recipe. The negative part equals

    p^m[(m+1)+(2m+1)p]/[4m(1+p)^2].

On the positive range use t=(p+z)/(1+z). Its endpoints are p and
T_*=[1+(m+1)p]/(m+1+p), and its integrand becomes exactly

    (m+1)/(4(1-p)^3) t^(m-1)
       [1+(m+1)p-(m+2)t]
       [1-(2m+5)p+(2m+4)t].                         (5)

In particular the second factor is as displayed; the earlier candidate's factor was incorrect. Expand the product in (5) as C_0+C_1t+C_2t^2 and set Q(t)=sum_(j=0)^2 C_j t^j/(m+j). Exact simplification gives

    Q(T_*)=-T_*^2 A(p)/[m(m+1)],

and

    [(m+1)+(2m+1)p]/[4m(1+p)^2]
       -(m+1)Q(p)/[4(1-p)^3]
      =p^2 D(p)/[m(1-p)^3(1+p)^2].

Here A,D use r=m+1. Multiply the first identity by (m+1)T_*^m/[4(1-p)^3] and the second by p^m to obtain (4). The verifier checks (5) directly from f_Z, both primitive identities, and (4)'s remaining algebra with m symbolic.

All denominators in (3)-(4) are positive for 0<p<1, so the derivative has the sign of L.

## 2. The initial range has positive derivative

D is strictly positive for p>=0. A is strictly increasing there, starts negative, and has a unique positive zero alpha in(0,1), since A(1)=4r+4>0. Thus L>0 for 0<p<=alpha.

For p>alpha define the positive ratio

    R(p)=4[p(r+p)/(1+rp)]^(r+1)
                       D(p)/[(1+p)^2A(p)].          (6)

Then L=(1+p)^2(1+rp)^(r+1) A(p)[R(p)-1]. We will show that R first decreases and then increases, with exactly one turning point.

## 3. A uniform degree-five sign certificate

Logarithmic differentiation of (6) gives

    R'(p)/R(p)
      =(p-1)^2 K_r(p)/
       [p(1+p)(r+p)(1+rp)D(p)A(p)],                (7)

where, in ascending powers,

    K_r(p)= -r^4-3r^3-2r^2
      +(-3r^4-9r^3-8r^2-4r)p
      +(r^4-5r^3-25r^2-9r+2)p^2
      +(11r^4-5r^3-21r^2-13r+4)p^3
      +(6r^4+4r^3-13r^2-3r)p^4
      +(2r^3+r^2-3r)p^5.

For r>=3 its coefficient signs are

    -, -, arbitrary, +, +, +.

The last three positive coefficients become, upon writing r=3+s, s>=0,

    [p^3]K=11s^4+127s^3+528s^2+914s+532,
    [p^4]K=6s^4+76s^3+347s^2+675s+468,
    [p^5]K=2s^3+19s^2+57s+54.

Thus there is exactly one sign change after zero coefficients are omitted. By Descartes' rule, counting multiplicity, K has at most one positive root. Its constant coefficient is negative and its leading coefficient is positive, so it has exactly one positive root, which is simple.

That root lies strictly above alpha. Indeed multiply the rational logarithmic derivative of (6) by its common denominator and put p=alpha. All terms vanish except the contribution from -A'/A, leaving

    (alpha-1)^2 K_r(alpha)
       =-alpha(1+alpha)(r+alpha)(1+r alpha)
                                      D(alpha)A'(alpha)<0.

Since alpha<1, this proves K_r(alpha)<0. Consequently (7) shows that R strictly decreases on(alpha,c) and strictly increases on(c,infinity), where c>alpha is the unique positive root of K. The additional derivative zero at p=1 does not change these monotonicity statements.

Finally,

    lim_(p down to alpha)R(p)=infinity,    R(1)=1.

If c>=1, then R>1 throughout(alpha,1). If c<1, its strict increase on(c,1) implies R(c)<1; hence it crosses one exactly once on(alpha,c), and stays below one on the rest of(alpha,1). Therefore R-1, and hence L, has at most one sign change on(alpha,1), only from positive to negative.

Together with Section 2, P_m' has at most one sign change on(0,1), only from positive to negative. The function either increases throughout or first increases and then decreases. Its minimum is therefore at an endpoint. Coupling the underlying exponentials proves continuity at both endpoints because the limiting comparisons have no atom at equality. This proves (1).

The argument and coefficient certificate hold for all m>=2. No finite parameter screen or numerical root location is used.
